summary: Adds a RObust Header Compression profile for compressing plain IP headers on their own, filling a gap left by the original ROHC framework in RFC 3095. That earlier document covered IP/UDP/RTP, IP/ESP and IP/UDP but not IP alone.

eli5.summary: A message with a long address on every page can use a short code instead. This document adds a short-code method for messages that only have the basic address part.

questions: header compression for ip packets without udp

how does rohc compress ip headers without udp
subtitle: A ROHC profile that compresses plain IP headers on their own, with no UDP or RTP above them.

tldr.problem: The original ROHC framework (RFC 3095) had profiles for IP/UDP/RTP, IP/ESP, IP/UDP and uncompressed streams, but none for IP alone. Traffic with only IP headers could not be compressed.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3843 defines profile 0x0004. It works like the IP/UDP profile with UDP removed, ends the static chain a different way, and can compress IP header chains of arbitrary length.
tldr.outcome: ROHC gains the missing IP-only piece. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 4815.

facts.label: Protocol values that continue the chain

today: RFC 3843 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 4815. It has not been obsoleted. It builds on RFC 3095 and has to be read together with it.

sections.title: The Gap in the ROHC Toolbox
sections.content:
RObust Header Compression (ROHC) is a framework defined in RFC 3095. It comes with profiles, which are compression protocols for particular header combinations: IP/UDP/RTP, IP/ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) and IP/UDP. It also has a profile for uncompressed packet streams.

The uncompressed profile lets ROHC carry any packet stream, so the lower layers do not need to multiplex different packet types. Its weakness, as the RFC notes, is that it does not compress the headers at all. Since all packets are expected to be IP packets and the IP header is often a major part of the total header, compressing just the IP header would be a useful alternative. RFC 3095 did not define such a profile, and this document fills that gap.

The new profile is described mainly as a list of differences from the IP/UDP profile, called ROHC UDP in this text. Unless the RFC says otherwise, mechanisms and formats are the same as for ROHC UDP.
sections.eli5: A toolbox had tools for fancy messages but not for plain ones. This document makes the missing tool.

sections.title: Ending the Chain and Handling Many IP Headers
sections.content:
In the IP/UDP profile, the static chain in an IR packet always ends with a UDP header part, which marks the boundary. With IP only there is no such last header. So the static chain ends when the Next Header / Protocol field of a static IP header part indicates anything other than IP (IPinIP or IPv6). The compressor may instead end the chain at any IP header by setting the most significant bit of the IP version field to 1, giving 0xC for IPv4 or 0xE for IPv6. The decompressor must store this in the context, and must restore the original version value in decompressed headers.

The second difference is depth. The compressed header formats of RFC 3095 carry at most two levels of IP headers, an inner and an outer. For the existing profiles, extra IP headers at best partly disable compression, because only IR and IR-DYN packets can be sent. The IP-only profile instead compresses any number of IP levels. It adds a chain of dynamic header information to the end of the compressed header, one entry for each IP header beyond the first two. The chain has the same structure as in IR and IR-DYN packets, and its length is inferred from the static chain in the context.
sections.eli5: When a letter has envelopes inside envelopes, this profile can still shorten every layer. It uses a special marker to say where the list of envelopes stops.

sections.title: Constant IP-ID
sections.content:
Most IPv4 stacks set the IP Identifier (IP-ID) from a counter that goes up by one per packet. ROHC UDP compresses that with offset IP-ID encoding based on the sequence number. Some stacks use a pseudo-random IP-ID, which is sent as-is. The RFC also notes that some IPv4 stacks use a constant IP-ID, which offset encoding cannot compress, so the whole field would have to be sent.

To avoid that cost, the dynamic part of the IPv4 header gets a new flag, SID (Static IP Identifier), in the same octet as DF, RND and NBO. For compressed headers other than IR and IR-DYN, the rules are:

  • If RND is 0 and SID is 0, the IP-ID uses offset IP-ID encoding with p = 0 and a default slope of 0.
  • If RND is 0 and SID is 1, the IP-ID is constant and compressed away; it is the value in the context.
  • If RND is 1, the IP-ID is sent uncompressed as additional octets at the end of the compressed header, after any extensions.

Only IR and IR-DYN packets can update the SID value in the context.
sections.eli5: If a number on every page never changes, you only need to say it once. Otherwise you would keep writing the same number again and again.

sections.title: Cancelling a Mode Transition
sections.content:
ROHC profiles run in modes: Unidirectional, Bi-directional Optimistic and Bi-directional Reliable. Compression starts in Unidirectional mode, and only the decompressor can ask for a change by sending feedback. Under RFC 3095 the compressor has to honour the request.

This profile redefines the Mode value 0 (in UOR-2, IR and IR-DYN packets) to mean Cancel Mode Transition. This lets the compressor decline a requested change. A decompressor that receives it MUST stay in its current mode and SHOULD avoid asking again for the declined mode for a certain amount of time.

The state variables C_TRANS, C_MODE, D_TRANS and D_MODE from RFC 3095 are adjusted. The compressor keeps C_MODE unchanged and sets C_TRANS to Pending when it gets a request. It sets it to Done when it receives an ACK for the cancelling packet. The decompressor keeps D_MODE unchanged and sets D_TRANS to Pending on the cancelling packet and to Done when a packet of type 1 or 0 for the unchanged mode arrives. Appendix A gives the detailed procedures for each transition direction. In every case the compressor must not send packet types 1 or 0 while C_TRANS is Pending.
sections.eli5: A friend asks to switch games, and you say "not now". They have to keep playing the current game and wait a while before asking again.

sections.title: Initializing the Context
sections.content:
The static context can be set up in two ways. The first is an IR packet naming profile 0x0004, whose static chain ends with an IP header part whose Next Header / Protocol field is anything other than IPinIP (4) or IPv6 (41), or whose version field signals termination. The second reuses an existing context with an IR-DYN packet for profile 0x0004, where the dynamic chain matches a prefix of the existing static chain and ends the same way.

In both cases the compressor initializes the sequence number (SN) to a random value when it sends the first IR or IR-DYN packet. The dynamic part is similar to ROHC UDP, with a two-octet SN at the end of the dynamic chain. Because the chains can be any length, the SN is added only once, at the end.
sections.eli5: Before using the short codes, both sides trade a full copy of the details once. After that, the short codes are enough.

sections.title: Packet Format and the CONTEXT_MEMORY Option
sections.content:
Apart from one new feedback option, the only packet format that differs from ROHC UDP is the general format of compressed packets. It has no UDP checksum at the end. Instead it ends with a list of dynamic chains, one for each IP header above the first two. These chains carry no SN, because the SN is already in the compressed base header.

The new feedback option is CONTEXT_MEMORY, with option type 9 and option length 0. It tells the compressor that the decompressor lacks the memory to handle the context of the stream as it is currently compressed. On receiving it, the compressor SHOULD compress the stream in a way that needs less decompressor memory, or stop compressing the stream.
sections.eli5: The receiver can wave a flag that says "my notebook is full". The sender then uses a simpler method or stops shortening.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC adds nothing new here. The security considerations of RFC 3095 apply equally to this document, without exceptions or additions.

For IANA, ROHC profile identifier 0x0004 has been reserved for this profile.
sections.eli5: The safety rules are the same as for the earlier document, and the profile gets its own number in the official list.
